title: Differentiating and Integrating Power Series
short: Work term by term inside the interval of convergence.

blocks.html: Inside its interval of convergence, a power series behaves like a polynomial: you can differentiate it and integrate it one term at a time. Starting from the geometric series, that produces series for $\ln(1 + x)$, $\arctan x$ and more.

Here is the idea. Differentiating $\sum c_n x^{n}$ term by term gives $\sum nc_nx^{n-1}$. The extra factor $n$ does not change the radius, because $\sqrt[n]{n} \to 1$, so the root test gives the same limit; integration divides by $n + 1$, which also leaves the radius alone. A theorem then guarantees that, for $|x| < R$, the new series really equals the derivative (or integral) of the function. Endpoints can change, so check them again.

If $f(x) = \sum c_n(x - a)^{n}$ for $|x - a| < R$, then on the same interval
$$f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} nc_n(x - a)^{n-1},$$ $$\int f(x)\,dx = C + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{c_n}{n + 1}(x - a)^{n+1}.$$

blocks.title: A logarithm
blocks.q: Find a power series for $\ln(1 + x)$.
steps: Integrate term by term: $\ln(1 + x) = C + x - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x^{3}}{3} - \cdots$.
At $x = 0$ both sides are 0, so $C = 0$: $\ln(1 + x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^{n}}{n}$, for $-1 < x \le 1$ (the endpoint $x = 1$ now converges).

blocks.title: Arctangent
blocks.q: Find a power series for $\arctan x$.
steps: Integrate: $\arctan x = C + x - \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{x^{5}}{5} - \cdots$, and $\arctan 0 = 0$ gives $C = 0$.
At $x = 1$: $\frac{\pi}{4} = 1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \cdots$, a famous (and very slowly converging) series for $\pi$.

blocks.name: taylor
blocks.cap: Partial sums of the series for $\ln(1 + x)$, built by integrating the geometric series. They match the curve on $(-1, 1]$; beyond $x = 1$ they swing wildly as you add terms.

blocks.html: Dropping the constant of integration. Integrating $\frac{1}{1 - x} = \sum x^{n}$ gives $-\ln(1 - x) = C + \sum\frac{x^{n+1}}{n + 1}$, and you find $C$ by plugging in the center: at $x = 0$, $-\ln 1 = 0 = C$. For other functions $C$ is not 0; for example, starting from $\int\frac{dx}{1 + x}$ to get $\ln(2 + x)$ would need $C = \ln 2$. Always evaluate both sides at the center.
